planting.note: Plant dormant cuttings or container vines in spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun; Chowan bears only female flowers, so plant a self-fertile pollinator such as Carlos or Cowart within 10-15 feet.

directions: Chowan is an early bronze-fruited muscadine released in the 1960s and long grown across the North Carolina and Virginia coastal plain, prized for its golden-bronze skin and classic musky-sweet muscadine flavor. Because Chowan carries only female flowers, plant it within 10-15 feet of a self-fertile cultivar such as Carlos or Cowart to ensure a full fruit set each season. The vigorous vine performs best trained onto a sturdy overhead arbor or high-wire trellis, where the loose clusters ripen through late summer and are picked individually as berries soften and detach easily. Like other muscadines, Chowan shrugs off the heat, humidity, and Pierce's disease pressure of the Gulf Coast that limit bunch-grape production.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

common_name: Hunt Muscadine Grape (Early-Ripening Black Female Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant dormant cuttings or container vines in spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun; Hunt is female-flowered and needs a self-fertile pollinator such as Carlos or Cowart planted nearby.

directions: Hunt is a black-skinned muscadine selected in 1920 at the Georgia Experiment Station in Experiment, Georgia, and remains a widely planted heirloom valued for its early ripening and high sugar content. The medium-large berries hang in good-sized clusters with medium-tough skin and rich, sweet flavor well suited to fresh eating, juice, jelly, and wine. Hunt carries only female flowers, so a self-fertile pollinator such as Carlos or Cowart must be planted nearby to secure reliable crops. The vine is notably vigorous and tolerant of heat, drought, and the fungal diseases that trouble bunch grapes in the humid Gulf South.

common_name: Mish Muscadine Grape (Heirloom Black Female Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant dormant cuttings or container vines in spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun; Mish bears only female flowers and requires a self-fertile pollinator such as Carlos or Cowart nearby.

directions: Mish is one of the old heirloom black muscadines selected from wild Southeastern vines generations before modern university breeding programs began, historically grouped with other early favorites such as Flowers, James, and Thomas for its combination of vigor, productivity, and dessert-quality fruit. The dark-skinned berries carry the rich, musky-sweet flavor prized in traditional muscadine cookery and fresh eating. Because Mish bears only female flowers, it needs a nearby self-fertile cultivar such as Carlos or Cowart to pollinate its blooms and set a full crop. Give it a sturdy arbor or high-wire trellis in full sun, where this tough, long-lived heirloom vine will thrive with minimal disease pressure through Gulf Coast summers.
sources: University of Georgia Muscadine Grape Breeding Program

common_name: Thomas Muscadine Grape (Historic Black Female Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant dormant cuttings or container vines in spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun; Thomas is female-flowered and must be planted alongside a self-fertile cultivar such as Carlos or Nesbitt.

directions: Thomas is a historic black muscadine selected from the wild well before the twentieth century, and it served as one of the foundational female parents in the University of Georgia's muscadine breeding program launched in 1909, contributing to the pedigree of later cultivars such as Magoon and, through further crosses, Noble. The dark, richly flavored berries retain the authentic musky-sweet character that defines classic Southern muscadine. Because Thomas is female-flowered, it must be planted alongside a self-fertile cultivar such as Carlos or Nesbitt to ensure pollination and fruit set. This vigorous heirloom vine remains available from specialty nurseries for gardeners who want a direct link to the earliest cultivated muscadines.
sources: University of Georgia Muscadine Grape Breeding Program

planting.note: Plant dormant cuttings or container vines in spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun; Dixieland is self-fertile and does not require a separate pollinator vine.

directions: Dixieland is a self-fertile bronze muscadine with medium-large berries, medium-tough skin, and excellent sweet flavor, making it a reliable choice where space allows for only one vine. It holds a notable place in muscadine breeding history as the pollen parent crossed with the black female cultivar Black Fry to produce the popular commercial cultivar Supreme. Yields can be somewhat uneven from year to year compared to the most productive modern releases, but fruit quality for fresh eating remains excellent. Train vines onto a sturdy arbor or trellis in full sun and well-drained soil, and prune hard each winter to renew the fruiting wood for the following season.

planting.note: Plant dormant cuttings or container vines in spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun; Eudora is female-flowered, so plant a self-fertile pollinator such as Southern Jewel or Delicious within 10-15 feet.

directions: Eudora is a female-flowered muscadine released by the University of Florida in 2006, bred for the fresh market and notable for its purple, oval berries that form in unusually tight clusters rather than the loose, few-berried sets typical of older cultivars. Each berry carries high sugar content and good eating texture, and the semi-recumbent vines show strong resistance to Pierce's disease and many of the fruit rots that plague muscadines in humid climates. Fruit ripens in midseason, typically late August along the Gulf Coast. Because Eudora carries only female flowers, plant it within 10-15 feet of a self-fertile cultivar such as Southern Jewel or Delicious to ensure good pollination and a full crop.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Oriole needs only about 100-200 chill hours, one of the lowest requirements of any astringent-type kaki cultivar, making it well suited to mild Gulf Coast winters.

directions: Oriole is a Korean-bred Asian persimmon valued for its very low chilling requirement, making it one of the more reliable astringent-type kaki selections for the mild winters of Gulf Coast gardens where many higher-chill cultivars bloom poorly. The tree bears heavy crops of large, deep red-orange to nearly black-fleshed fruit with an intensely sweet flavor once fully soft-ripe. Because Oriole is an astringent type, the fruit must soften completely to a jelly-like texture before eating, unlike non-astringent Fuyu-type persimmons that can be eaten while still firm. Provide consistent summer moisture to prevent premature fruit drop and grow in full sun on well-drained soil for the best production.

common_name: Cardinal Persimmon (Non-Astringent Korean Persimmon, syn. 'Jo Choo')

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Cardinal is non-astringent and can be harvested and eaten firm, without waiting for the fruit to soften.

directions: Cardinal, grown under the cultivar name Jo Choo in its native Korea, is a non-astringent Asian persimmon that can be eaten firm and crisp straight off the tree, without the softening required by astringent types like Hachiya or Eureka. The compact tree produces large, sweet, orange fruit that ripens early in the season, and its naturally smaller stature makes it a good fit for home gardens with limited space. Vivid orange-red fall foliage adds ornamental value after the fruit is harvested. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, and expect the tree to perform well in the mild winters typical of zone 9a Gulf Coast gardens.
